title: Sangrand at home
hookLine: marking the new month with a reading
tomorrow: a year of gurpurabs, lived. what's left to plan?

lines: A NEW BILL, A FRESH PAGE.
A SONG WITH A STANZA PER MONTH.
cards: A new month usually means a new bill, a fresh page on the wall calendar, a reminder to change the air filter. Here's something odd in the Granth.

Guru Arjan wrote a song of the months, the Barah Maha, with a stanza for each month in turn. Then, near the end, he says no month is special in itself. So why would anyone keep a reading for the first day of the month?

teach.b: The day is Sangrand, when the sun moves into a new sign and the Punjabi solar month begins.

On it, some gurdwaras and some homes read that month's stanza of the Barah Maha, so the month opens with its own verse. Each stanza turns a season toward the soul. In Chet, it says, remembering the Lord brings deep joy.
In Vaisakh, it asks how anyone parted from love can be patient. Now the puzzle.
Near the close, on Ang one thirty-six, Guru Arjan says, in paraphrase: the months, the days, the moments are blessed for those on whom the Lord's glance of grace falls. So the date isn't magic.
What makes a day good is remembering in it. Sikhs live that out two ways.

teach.h: A DOORWAY, OR EVERY DAY ALIKE.
teach.b: Some love Sangrand as a doorway: a set time to begin the month with its verse, at home or in sangat. Others prefer not to treat any date as holier than another, and say every day is the same before God.
Both lean on the same line, and both agree on what it asks: whatever the date, begin it remembering. That's what a reading at home on Sangrand does.
It opens a month with a line instead of a to-do list.

how: On Sangrand, the first day of the Punjabi solar month, some gurdwaras hold a special diwan where the month's stanza of the Barah Maha (Majh, Guru Arjan) is read; some families read it at home, while other Sikhs keep no special observance for the date.

o: a fast kept on the first day of each new month
marking the new month at home with that month's verse
a monthly family meeting about the budget

games.q: the month and its verse — tap the pairs.
p: the day a Punjabi solar month begins
Guru Arjan's song of the months
remembering the Lord brings deep joy
blessed for those on whom grace falls

s: the Barah Maha says some months are luckier than others
near its close, Guru Arjan says the months and moments are blessed for those on whom grace falls.
Sangrand is the day a Punjabi solar month begins
the sun moves into a new sign, and the month opens.
every Sikh treats Sangrand as a holy day
some love it as a doorway; others treat every day alike. both lean on the same line.

games.q: your cousin says reading on Sangrand is superstition, since the Granth says no date is special. what's the fairest reply?
o: the date isn't magic; the reading is a set time to begin the month remembering.
she's wrong: the first of the month carries a special blessing in itself.
she's right: the Barah Maha has nothing to do with the months at all.
games.why: Guru Arjan says the days are blessed where grace falls, not by the calendar. Sangrand keepers and those who skip it lean on the same line.

practice: Find this month's stanza, in a gutka, an app or a printed Barah Maha, or choose any line of Gurbani you know. Copy one line by hand, slowly, in whatever script you can.
Then rest your eyes on what you wrote, and breathe with it until the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: Sangrand at home. Marking the first day of the Punjabi month with a reading, often that month's stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha.

orig.note: Punjabi form of sankranti: the sun's move into a new sign, the first day of the month.

carryVoice: Something to keep: a new month, opened with a line before the list. That's day 1759.
